issues.legal_issue: A court may direct the sale of property held by a court-appointed receiver to resident occupants offering a higher competitive price when no completed sale or accrued purchaser’s right prevents that result and the transaction serves a broader social benefit without depriving another party of an accrued legal right.
material_facts: A receiver appointed by the court held the disputed property and was authorized to sell it by private treaty with the parties’ approval.

A prospective purchaser offered a lower price, paid only part of it for several months, and offered to buy only on terms inconsistent with the owners’ condition that the property be purchased subject to pending litigation.
The occupants and their families had been living on the property and had built permanent structures there.
The occupants offered a higher price and undertook to pay the balance and purchase despite the pending litigation.
The earlier transaction had not become a completed sale, and the prospective purchaser had no accrued legal right that would be deprived by accepting the higher offer.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the direction to sell the property to the occupants and their nominees, subject to payment of the stated price and their agreement to purchase notwithstanding the pending litigation; it modified the time for payment of the balance and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Social justice may support preferring a transaction benefiting a larger number where it causes no serious detriment to another party and deprives nobody of an accrued legal right. A receiver appointed under Order XL Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure may sell property on the court’s direction, including by private negotiation; the court must exercise its discretion to secure a fair sale. The Court referred to the constitutional Preamble, Kayjay Industries (P) Ltd. v. Asnew Drums (P) Ltd., Tarinikamal Pandit v. Prafulla Kumar Chatterjee, and Everest Coal Company (P) Ltd. v. State of Bihar.

rule.if: receiver_sale_dispute and no_completed_sale and substantial_balance_unpaid and higher_competitive_offer and many_families_in_residence and no_accrued_right_deprived

predicates.receiver_sale_dispute: The dispute concerns a proposed sale of property held by a court-appointed receiver.
predicates.no_completed_sale: The proposed sale to the earlier prospective purchaser has not been completed.
predicates.substantial_balance_unpaid: The earlier prospective purchaser has left a substantial part of the offered price unpaid when the competing offer is considered.
predicates.higher_competitive_offer: The resident occupants offer a higher price on terms acceptable to the property’s owners or the court.
predicates.many_families_in_residence: A substantial number of families are living on the property and would be affected by its sale to someone else.
predicates.no_accrued_right_deprived: Accepting the competing offer would not deprive another party of an accrued legal right.

issues.definition: When a receiver-sale dispute has no completed earlier sale, the earlier buyer has left a substantial balance unpaid, resident occupants make a higher competitive offer, many families live on the property, and no accrued right would be deprived, the higher offer may be accepted for the resident occupants.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court should not use its discretionary jurisdiction to interfere with a fact-sensitive sale direction when the lower appellate court has applied social-justice considerations without breaching the law.
material_facts: The matter reached the Supreme Court by special leave under Article 136.
The lower appellate court directed sale to resident occupants who offered more than the earlier prospective purchaser, whose sale had not been completed.
The majority considered that the decision caused no deprivation of an accrued legal right and breached no law.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere under Article 136 and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 confers discretionary jurisdiction, and the Court should not interfere with a lower appellate court’s decision where its approach recognizes human needs, causes no deprivation of accrued legal rights, and breaches no law. The Court relied on the constitutional Preamble’s commitment to social, economic, and political justice.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and fact_sensitive_social_justice_order and no_law_breached and no_accrued_right_deprived

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter is an appeal brought by special leave to the Supreme Court.
predicates.fact_sensitive_social_justice_order: The lower appellate court made a discretionary order after weighing social needs and the circumstances of the affected people.
predicates.no_law_breached: The lower appellate court’s approach does not breach an applicable legal rule.
predicates.no_accrued_right_deprived: The order does not deprive a party of an accrued legal right.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal, when the challenged order is fact-sensitive, breaches no law, and deprives nobody of an accrued legal right, the Supreme Court declines to intervene.

issues.legal_issue: Proceedings concerning possession under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure do not determine title to the disputed property, although they reflect possession.
material_facts: Proceedings under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure concerning possession of the property were pending.
The parties disputed who possessed the property, and the possession proceedings did not adjudicate title.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the pendency of the proceedings, and any order made in them, does not affect title but reflects the fact of possession.
issues.legal_principle: Section 145(4) requires the magistrate to determine possession without reference to the merits of the parties’ claims to a right to possess; Section 145(6) permits an order declaring entitlement to possession until eviction in due course of law. Such proceedings do not determine title. The Court relied on Bhinka v. Charan Singh.

predicates.criminal_possession_proceeding: A criminal proceeding is brought to resolve a dispute about possession of land or other property.

issues.definition: When a criminal proceeding concerns possession of property, the proceeding may reflect possession but does not determine title.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot acquire title or a right in property merely by entering or remaining on property held in the custody of a court-appointed receiver without leave, consent, or court sanction.
material_facts: A court-appointed receiver took possession of the property and continued to hold it for the court.
The occupants entered or remained on the property after the receiver had taken possession, without obtaining leave or consent from the receiver or sanction from the court.
The occupants relied on their presence on the property in seeking a benefit in the proposed sale.
issues.conclusion: The Court stated that interference with a receiver’s possession should not be encouraged and that no party acquires title or a right merely by coming onto or remaining on property in the receiver’s possession without authorization.
issues.legal_principle: Property in the possession of a receiver appointed under Order XL of the Code of Civil Procedure is in the custody of the court; interference with that possession is not to be encouraged, and unauthorized entry does not confer title or a right. The Court relied on Everest Coal Company (P) Ltd. v. State of Bihar and referred to Halsbury’s Laws of England and Kerr on Receivers.

predicates.property_in_receiver_custody: A court-appointed receiver has taken possession of the property and holds it for the court.
predicates.unauthorized_entry_or_occupation: A party enters or remains on the property without the receiver’s leave or consent or the court’s sanction.

issues.definition: When property is held by a court-appointed receiver and a party enters or remains without authorization, that entry or occupation confers no title or right.
